title: Hardware
description: The machine, for one GPU, many, or none: what it has, how busy it is, where the models run, and what holds them back (heat, memory, the CPU).

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: The processor's model, as the kernel names it (node-exporter's CPU info).

panels.title: Cores
panels.description: Physical cores, and the threads the system schedules on them (logical CPUs). A model on the CPU runs a thread per physical core.

panels.title: RAM
panels.description: The machine's memory.

panels.title: GPUs
panels.description: The GPUs nvidia-smi reports, by model.

panels.title: VRAM
panels.description: All the GPUs' memory together.

panels.title: Up for
panels.description: Since the machine last started.

panels.title: CPU busy
panels.description: All cores together, over the last 5 minutes. A model running on the CPU keeps this high while it answers.

panels.title: Memory used by programs
panels.description: Memory that programs hold and the system cannot take back (100% minus MemAvailable). The models' files that the engine maps sit in the page cache, not here: Memory below shows it. When a model is bigger than RAM and the GPU, that page cache is full and the model is read from disk as it runs (Admin -> Models).

panels.title: GPUs busy
panels.description: The GPUs' average. Each GPU's own is under GPUs below.

panels.title: VRAM used
panels.description: All the GPUs' memory together. vLLM and SGLang take their share of a GPU when they start, so a GPU they run on sits high and flat.

panels.title: Hottest GPU
panels.description: The hottest GPU now. Past about 85 °C most cards slow themselves down.

panels.title: Hottest CPU sensor
panels.description: The hottest CPU sensor now (cpu-temp-exporter).

panels.title: GPU power
panels.description: What all the GPUs draw now, and their limits together.

panels.title: Loaded models
panels.description: Each loaded model, where it sits (its GPUs, or RAM) and the memory the app reckons it takes there: a model split over several GPUs has a line for each. 0 where the app does not know its size (the model named in .env).

panels.title: GPUs
panels.emptyText: No GPU reports here, so the models run on the CPU: the CPU and Memory sections below are what set their speed. A machine with NVIDIA GPUs shows each of them here once the gpu-exporter runs (it does wherever the NVIDIA driver is installed).

panels.description: One line per GPU, now. Busy and VRAM fill their bars; Slowed down is 1 while the GPU holds its clocks back for heat or a power brake (the normal power limit is not counted); power limits and fans are on GPU Hardware. PCIe below its card's best (a gen or lanes lower than the others) slows loading and multi-GPU work.

options.content: Clocks, PCIe traffic, fans, memory errors and NVIDIA's data-centre detail (DCGM): the [GPU Hardware](/admin/dashboards/gpu-hardware) dashboard.

panels.title: CPU busy, by kind of work
panels.description: During GPU inference the CPU should be mostly idle. Sustained `user` or `system` load often means the model fell back to CPU, or tokenisation is the bottleneck.

targets.expr: sum by (mode) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="idle"}[5m])) / on() group_left count(count by (cpu) (node_cpu_seconds_total))

panels.title: Cores: busiest, average, quietest
panels.description: Three lines however many cores the machine has. Busiest far above average: one thread does the work (a single-threaded step). All three high: the CPU is the limit. Each core's own: Show as table.

panels.title: Waiting for a CPU
panels.description: The share of time at least one task was ready to run but waited for a CPU (the kernel's pressure figures). Above about 20% for long, the CPU is what holds the work back.

panels.title: Load per CPU
panels.description: The load average divided by the logical CPUs: 1 is every CPU busy, above 1 work queues for them.

panels.title: CPU clock
panels.description: The cores' clock over each minute, against the most it can reach. Low under load means it is held back (heat, power).

panels.title: CPU temperature
panels.description: The hottest CPU sensor and the average of all of them, from the cpu-temp-exporter: two lines whatever the core count. A gap between them is one core or one die running hot; CPU temperature per sensor, below, shows which. Linux reads coretemp/k10temp via hwmon; Windows scrapes LibreHardwareMonitor on the host.

targets.legendFormat: page cache (the models’ files, and others)

panels.title: Swapping
panels.description: Memory moved to and from the swap disk. Lasting swapping slows a model on the CPU many times over: lower its context or load a smaller model.

panels.title: Waiting for memory
panels.description: The share of time tasks waited for memory to be freed (the kernel's pressure figures). Above a few percent, RAM is too small for what runs.

panels.title: NVMe temperature
panels.description: Each NVMe drive's composite temperature (SMART temp1) from node-exporter's hwmon collector, which reads the kernel's own nvme sensors -- node-exporter already mounts the host /sys, so no extra exporter is needed. A drive is named by its device, then the model it reports (node_nvme_info), as in nvme0 · <model>, or by its device alone when it reports no model. Some drives also report their NAND and controller as temp2/temp3, which the composite lags under sustained writes. SATA drives have no sensor here.

targets.expr: label_join(label_replace(node_hwmon_temp_celsius{chip=~"nvme_nvme[0-9]+",sensor="temp1"}, "device", "$1", "chip", "^nvme_(nvme[0-9]+)$") * on (instance, device) group_left (model) max by (instance, device, model) (node_nvme_info{model!=""}), "drive", " · ", "device", "model") or on (instance, chip) label_replace(node_hwmon_temp_celsius{chip=~"nvme_nvme[0-9]+",sensor="temp1"}, "drive", "$1", "chip", "^nvme_(nvme[0-9]+)$")
